title: A Weekend for Two: A Marriage Retreat
subtitle: Five sessions for a married couple away together, or for a church retreat: to remember, tell the truth, repair, delight, and promise again.
audience: married couples at any stage, newly married or long married, on their own or at a church retreat, and the pastors who lead them
intro:
Two people who once talked until the small hours can become two people who talk mostly about the calendar, the bills, the house, and whose turn it is. Hardly anyone chooses it. Life fills up, and love that isn't tended goes quiet long before it goes cold. The church hasn't always helped. We talk about marriage at weddings and in emergencies and leave the long middle mostly alone. I'm a pastor, so that's my indictment as much as anyone's.

Scripture knows how easily people forget, and it built an answer into Israel's year. At the Feast of Tabernacles, God's people left their houses and lived for seven days in booths made of branches, rejoicing before the LORD, so that their descendants would know he had made Israel live in booths when he brought them out of Egypt (Leviticus 23:40-43). A people who never stopped would soon forget, and God made remembering a feast.

This guide is a small version of that for a marriage: a weekend away, or a church retreat, given to five conversations. You'll remember how you began, tell each other the truth about where you are now, repair what can be repaired, recover some delight, and make your promises again, this time knowing what they cost.

It's written for couples at any stage: two years in and surprised by how hard it is; ten years in with small children and little sleep, or without the children you hoped for; twenty-five years in with teenagers and aging parents pulling from both sides; or forty years in with a quiet house and a question about who you are now. If things are good and you'd like to keep them that way, this is for you. If you're tired or hurt, or not sure your spouse still wants this, it's for you too. And if you came only because your spouse asked, and you aren't sure what you believe about any of it, you're welcome here as you are. Nobody is grading this weekend. It asks only that you tell the truth.

A weekend won't fix a marriage, and this guide won't pretend it can. What it can do is stop the drift long enough for two people to look at each other again.
howToUse:
The five sessions follow a weekend: Friday evening, three on Saturday, and Sunday morning. Each takes about ninety minutes. If you can't get away, use five evenings at home, phones in another room. Print a copy for each of you.

Read the opening and the Scripture aloud together, then go apart to answer the questions under *Each of you, on your own*; one true sentence is worth more than a careful page. Come back for *Together*. Either of you may pass on any question; say so rather than faking an answer. Nothing your spouse writes here may be used against them later.

At a church retreat, a leader can read the opening and Scripture aloud before couples go off to write and talk. No one should be asked to share what they or their spouse wrote. Leaders, read the care note first, and make it easy for anyone to find you alone. If someone tells you they're afraid of their spouse, believe them, don't tell the spouse or meet with them as a couple, and help them reach the Hotline below.

If one of you doesn't share the other's faith, the Scripture is here to show what Christians read, not to corner you, and where a session suggests prayer, you can simply listen.

For pastors and their spouses: the church can wait for a weekend. Find someone to cover, and turn the phones off. Jesus took his disciples away to rest when the crowds left them no time to eat (Mark 6:31). The ministry is not the marriage, and a church is better served by a pastor whose home is honest than by one whose marriage gets the leftovers. If one of you has been carrying the church without the title, this is the weekend to say so.
careNote: This workbook is for two people who are safe with each other. If either of you is afraid of the other, or feels controlled, watched, threatened, or pressured, sexually or in any other way, stop here. Talk alone with someone you trust, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline in the box below, and don't do couples work with a partner you fear. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911. A weekend away is also the wrong place to disclose or work through an addiction, abuse, or an affair, especially one only recently discovered. Those need a licensed counselor, and where there's danger, the Hotline. If you're grieving the recent loss of a child, a parent, or a pregnancy, begin with whichever session feels gentlest, and skip whatever doesn't fit.
closing:
By Monday the dishes will be back, and the calendar, and the old habits that turn two people into strangers. Israel went home from the Feast of Tabernacles to their fields and flocks, and the feast came round again the next year. A weekend works the same way. It can't hold a marriage together on its own, but it can set a pattern you return to.

If this weekend brought up more than the two of you can carry, that isn't a failure. It shows you where you need help. Call a counselor this week, and if you're afraid, call the Hotline listed at the front of this workbook. And if one of you came unconvinced about God and leaves unconvinced, you still told each other the truth this weekend, which is the one thing it asked of you.

You'll forget again. Everyone does, which is why God gave Israel feasts and Jesus gave his church a meal. On the night he was betrayed, he took bread and told his disciples to do this in remembrance of him (1 Corinthians 11:23-24). He knew we would forget, so he made remembering something we do together, with our hands, again and again. A marriage is kept the same way, in small acts repeated long after the feeling of a weekend fades.

The promises you made again are still too big for you. They always were. That's why you made them before God, who keeps his promises when we don't keep ours, and who hasn't forgotten a word you said.

sessions.title: Remember how you began
sessions.why:
First, plainly: this weekend is for two people who are safe with each other. If either of you is afraid of the other, or feels controlled, watched, threatened, or pressured, including sexually, stop here, even if your spouse wants to go on, and don't do couples work with a partner you fear. You don't owe anyone an explanation. Talk alone with someone you trust, from a phone your spouse can't check, and call the National Domestic Violence Hotline in the box headed *If anyone is in danger* near the front of this workbook. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911.

It's Friday evening. You've probably arrived tired, and maybe you argued in the car. Problems can wait until morning. Tonight, start where Scripture keeps telling God's people to start, with remembering.

In Deuteronomy, Moses stands with Israel at the edge of the promised land and tells them to remember the whole road: forty years in the wilderness, the hunger, the manna, the clothes that didn't wear out. He's worried about what comes next. Once they're settled, with fine houses and growing herds, their hearts will grow proud and they'll forget the God who brought them out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 8:11-14). Marriages forget the same way. The full, busy years can do it as surely as the hard ones, when two people stop telling their story and start running a household.

Psalm 103, which bears David's name, opens with a man talking to his own soul, telling it not to forget God's kind deeds, and the list is honest. It includes sins forgiven and a life pulled back from the Pit. You don't get rescued from a pit you were never in. Tonight you'll tell the story of your marriage, the sweet parts and the hard ones, a hospital room or a year you almost didn't make it. Tell the hard parts truthfully. Remembering in Scripture isn't nostalgia. It's learning to see the whole road as one road, with God on it.

scripture.text: Remember that these forty years the LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments. He humbled you, and in your hunger He gave you manna to eat, which neither you nor your fathers had known, so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD. Your clothing did not wear out and your feet did not swell during these forty years.

Bless the LORD, O my soul; all that is within me, bless His holy name. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds— He who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the Pit and crowns you with loving devotion and compassion, who satisfies you with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.

questions: What do you remember about the moment you knew this was serious? Write enough that your spouse would recognize the room.
What did you think marriage would be like? Where has it turned out harder than you expected, and where has it turned out better?
What did you love about your spouse at the beginning that you've stopped telling them? Is it still true?
Name the hardest stretch you've come through together. What do you think your spouse was carrying then that you didn't see at the time?
What has your spouse done for you, maybe years ago, that you've never properly thanked them for? What did it cost them?
Where do you see God's hand in your story so far, and where can't you see it yet? If you aren't sure God was in it, write what you're grateful for that neither of you earned.
sessions.together:
Read your answers aloud, one question at a time, taking turns going first. Tonight is mostly for listening. If your spouse remembers something differently, don't correct them; ask about it. Each of you has kept part of the marriage in memory, and your spouse may be holding something you thought was lost. If either of you was married before, or your marriage began in a hard place, the story may start with an ending. Tell as much of it as helps the other understand you, and no more.

Spend the most time on the hardest stretch. Tell your spouse what you think they were carrying then, and let them tell you how close you came. Then say the thank-you you wrote down, out loud and in detail. Most of us thank strangers more easily than the person we live with.

To finish, read the psalm again slowly. If you both pray, thank God for the mercies you named tonight, one by one. If one of you doesn't pray, take turns saying one thing from your story you never want to forget. Then stop. Whatever is wrong will still be there in the morning, and you'll face it better for having slept.
sessions.practice: Sleep, and if one of you wakes early, let the other rest. Sometime before the next session, take ten minutes alone and finish this sentence in writing as many times as you honestly can: *Something I've stopped saying to you is...* It doesn't need to be dramatic; small things count. Don't share it yet. Bring it with you.

sessions.title: Tell the truth about now
sessions.why:
It's Saturday morning, and this is the harder conversation. Married people can go years without telling each other a lie and still stop telling each other the truth. The first things to go are particular sentences: the hurt that didn't seem worth a fight, the worry about money or the doctor's call, the loneliness that would sound like an accusation, the hope you set aside because there was no room for it. Most of those silences begin as kindness or tiredness. Years later you're living beside someone you no longer quite know, and who no longer quite knows you.

The Teacher in Ecclesiastes describes a man who works without end and has no one, and who finally asks for whom he's toiling (Ecclesiastes 4:8). Then he praises two together, companions of any kind, though each of his examples fits a marriage. Notice what they need. You can't lift a companion whose fall you know nothing about, and two people can lie side by side and still be cold. It's possible to be two hard workers sharing a house, one quietly down and the other with no idea. Christians have long heard God in the third strand of the cord, though the Teacher may mean only that three are stronger than two. Either way, a cord holds because its strands are bound together, and silence is how they come apart.

Proverbs calls an honest answer a kiss on the lips, and it also knows that rash words pierce like a sword. The aim this morning is truth that heals rather than truth that wins, and it starts with the truth about yourself. Most of us, and I don't exempt myself, find it far easier to tell the truth about the people we live with than about ourselves.

scripture.text: Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor. For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up; but pity the one who falls without another to help him up! Again, if two lie down together, they will keep warm; but how can one keep warm alone? And though one may be overpowered, two can resist. Moreover, a cord of three strands is not quickly broken.
An honest answer given is like a kiss on the lips.
Speaking rashly is like a piercing sword, but the tongue of the wise brings healing.

questions: What has changed between you in the last few years that neither of you has said out loud?
Is there a worry you've been carrying alone, about money, health, work, or family? What has kept you from telling your spouse?
When do you feel most alone in your marriage? Be specific about the time of day and the kind of moment.
What do you suspect your spouse is carrying right now that you haven't asked about?
What have you wanted from your marriage and quietly stopped asking for?
What haven't you said about faith, your own or your spouse's? It might be a doubt you carry or a pressure you feel.
How do you make it hard for your spouse to tell you the truth? If you aren't sure, write what you think they would say.
sessions.together:
Take turns, one question at a time. The listener's first job is to understand, not to reply. Say back what you heard in your own words and ask, *Is there more?* You'll want to explain or defend yourself. Wait until your spouse says you've understood; there may be less to defend than you thought.

Then read each other the sentences you wrote about what you've stopped saying. Choose one or two that matter most to each of you, and talk about what it would take to say them freely again. Give real time to the last question, because the answer is in your own hands.

If voices rise, stop, agree on a time to come back, and keep it. Anything that leaves either of you afraid ends the workbook there. And if one of you has been low for weeks, sleeping badly or finding no joy in anything, take that to a doctor or counselor, and if either of you has been thinking about ending your life, use the crisis lines at the front of this workbook today.

If what you've stopped saying is an affair, an addiction, or abuse, this isn't the morning for it; read the care note again. If you've been hiding it, don't let that become one more reason to keep hiding; call a counselor this week. If you're the one being hurt, call the Hotline and keep your plans private until you're safe.
sessions.practice: Before this afternoon, take twenty minutes alone. Pray the end of Psalm 139, asking God to search you and show you any offensive way in you, and ask him where you've hurt your spouse, not where they've hurt you. It's for owning your own wrongs, not for taking on blame that isn't yours. If you don't pray, sit quietly with the same question. Write down what comes, and bring it to the next session.

sessions.title: Repair what you can
sessions.why:
It's Saturday afternoon, and the morning may have stirred up hurts, new and old. Two sinners living at close range will wound each other, sometimes without meaning to and sometimes on purpose.

Whatever else it is, forgiveness gives up your claim to make your spouse pay and hands the debt to God, who forgave you first. It isn't the same as trust or silence, and it never asks anyone to stay within reach of harm. Trust is rebuilt slowly, by evidence, on the hurt person's timetable. Reconciliation takes both of you and asks the one who did the harm to own it without excuses. Agreeing never to mention it again is only a truce, and wounds kept under a truce seldom heal.

Christians differ on whether forgiveness waits for repentance. Some say it does, since Jesus says to forgive a brother who repents (Luke 17:3-4), and find comfort in a forgiveness that never pretends a wrong away. Others say it doesn't, since he says to forgive whatever you hold against anyone when you pray (Mark 11:25), and find comfort in not having to wait on the one who hurt you. Settle it with your pastor and your church.

The letter to the Colossians asks a church to bear with one another and to forgive. It doesn't say which complaint needs which, but at home it matters: temperament, the lateness or the bluntness, needs bearing with; a real wrong needs forgiveness. Treat a quirk as a sin and you'll wear the marriage out; treat a sin as a quirk and it will fester.

Old wounds come back, and old fears. Years after Joseph wept over his brothers and kissed them, their father died, and they were afraid all over again that he'd pay them back. Joseph wept again, then answered honestly: he called what they did evil, refused to take God's place, and promised to provide for them. When the past returns at a funeral, a diagnosis, or a child leaving home, that doesn't prove the forgiveness was false. Sometimes it has to be spoken again.

scripture.text: Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity.
Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you.

When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him.” ... But Joseph replied, “Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God? As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people. Therefore do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” So Joseph reassured his brothers and spoke kindly to them.

questions: What in your spouse do you need to bear with rather than forgive? Have you been treating it as a wrong?
Is there something you say you've forgiven when really you've only stopped mentioning it? What does it still cost you?
Where have you hurt your spouse in a way you've never fully owned? Write the first two sentences of the apology, without the word *but*.
Is there an old wound between you that comes back at certain times? What tends to bring it back?
If you've been forgiven for something, what would help you believe it? If you've been hurt, what would help you trust again?
After a fight, who usually moves first to make peace, and how? Is that working for both of you?
sessions.together:
Begin with apologies. Whoever wrote down a hurt they caused goes first. Name it plainly, what you did and what you think it cost, and say you're sorry with no *but* attached. Then ask, *Is there anything I'm missing?* and listen to the answer. If you caused the hurt, don't be the one to say God brought good out of it; that's for the one you hurt to say, if they ever do. The one who was hurt doesn't have to forgive on the spot, and it's honest to say, *I want to forgive you, and I'm not there yet.* Then switch.

Tell each other what you've decided to bear with, and agree to stop treating it as a crime. Then turn to the old wound, if there is one, and decide together what it needs. Some old wounds need forgiveness spoken aloud again, or time and evidence, and the one who caused the hurt can ask what evidence would help. Some need a counselor; saying so is wisdom, not failure. If the wound is abuse, or an affair or addiction you haven't yet worked through with a counselor, stop here and follow the care note.

If you pray, pray for each other by name, and for the wound by name. Then rest. Repair is tiring.
sessions.practice: Before supper, do something restful that has nothing to do with your marriage's troubles, a nap or a walk. Then dress for dinner a little better than you need to, the way you might have when you were first going out. If something from this afternoon is still raw, say so kindly instead of pretending. Delight doesn't require that everything be settled.

sessions.title: Delight in each other
sessions.why:
It's Saturday evening. If the afternoon was heavy, that's all the more reason for this session. Delight isn't the reward for finishing the hard conversations. It's part of what marriage is for, and it's often the first thing a tired couple gives up.

Scripture is less embarrassed about this than the church has often been, preachers included. Near the middle of the Bible sits a book of love poetry, the Song of Songs, in which each lover invites the other away. He calls her to come away with him because winter is over and the vines are in blossom. She asks him to go with her to the countryside for the night and promises her love there. In the chapter where she calls him her beloved and her friend, the poem tells of a night she was slow to open the door, and when she did, he had gone (Song of Songs 5:2-6). Tired lovers miss each other. She went looking for him.

Delight has several rooms. There's friendship, simply enjoying each other's company. There's play, which some couples haven't had in years. And there's physical love, which Scripture treats as a gift. Bodies change with illness, childbirth, surgery, grief, medication, and age, and it's natural to feel shy about a body that no longer looks or works the way it did. Love that lasts learns to praise the body in front of it, not the one in the wedding photos.

Some things come into a marriage bed from outside it. The past comes in, sexual history and sometimes sexual harm done to you long before you met, and pornography comes in from a screen. None of it makes you unlovable, harm done to you was never your fault, and none of it has to be carried alone. And nothing tonight is owed on demand. Paul wrote about the marriage bed in both directions and made even time apart a matter of mutual consent (1 Corinthians 7:3-5). Nothing there licenses pressure or force. Delight can be offered and received. It can't be demanded.

scripture.text: My beloved calls to me, “Arise, my darling. Come away with me, my beautiful one. For now the winter is past; the rain is over and gone. The flowers have appeared in the countryside; the season of singing has come, and the cooing of turtledoves is heard in our land. The fig tree ripens its figs; the blossoming vines spread their fragrance. Arise, come away, my darling; come away with me, my beautiful one.”
His mouth is most sweet; he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.

I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me. Come, my beloved, let us go to the countryside; let us spend the night among the wildflowers. Let us go early to the vineyards to see if the vine has budded, if the blossom has opened, if the pomegranates are in bloom— there I will give you my love.

questions: When did the two of you last laugh together, really laugh? What were you doing?
What do you enjoy doing with your spouse that has nothing to do with work, the house, or the children?
If you had a free day together with nothing you had to do, how would you want to spend it?
What do you find beautiful in your spouse now that you couldn't have seen when you were younger?
Has your body changed in a way that makes you shy with your spouse? What would help you feel at ease again?
What's one thing about touch, affection, or sex that you've wanted to say and haven't? Write it as a wish, not a complaint.
Is anything making closeness hard right now, such as exhaustion, pain, grief, or an old hurt? You don't have to share all of it tonight.
sessions.together:
Start with the easy questions and enjoy them. Then plan one thing, tonight or tomorrow, that's purely for fun, and do it.

When you talk about the physical side of your marriage, use the wishes you wrote, the kind that begin *I'd love it if*. Listen for what's under your spouse's words, which may be a longing to be wanted or a fear of being judged. If either of you wrote about something painful, thank them for telling you, and don't try to solve it tonight. When sex has become painful or physically difficult, a doctor is the right first call, and this guide isn't medical advice. When old harm comes back as fear or as memories that won't leave, a licensed counselor can help, and so can the sexual assault hotline at the front of this workbook. And if pornography has been part of your marriage, tonight isn't the night to confess it or argue about it. That conversation goes better with a counselor or pastor beside you, so before the weekend ends, decide when you'll have it, and with whom. The care page at livewellbyjamesbell.co/help/pornography is a place to start.

Then put the workbook away. What happens next, if anything, belongs to the two of you and no one else. Either of you can say no, or not tonight, and that answer stands without sulking or pressure. If either of you is too tired or too sad for more than holding hands, holding hands is enough.
sessions.practice: Before the morning, find the words you said at your wedding if you have them, the vows or the order of service. If you can't, write down what you remember promising. Bring them to the last session, and sleep in if you can.

sessions.title: Make your promises again
sessions.why:
It's Sunday morning. Most couples make their wedding vows with little idea of what they're promising. That's the nature of a vow: it binds a future you can't see. But you know more now. You know what the years have brought, the jobs and the illnesses, the children or the empty rooms, and you know your spouse's temper and tenderness, and your own. This morning you'll make the same promise with your eyes open, and give it a shape: a simple rule of life, the kind Christians have long kept, a few practices chosen ahead of time so that love isn't left to whatever energy remains at the end of the day.

The words many couples hear at weddings come from Ruth, and they weren't first spoken at one. A widow from Moab said them to her widowed mother-in-law on the road to Judah, after Naomi had urged her again and again to go home. There was no husband in view for Ruth and only a foreign country ahead, and Naomi was so grieved that she would soon ask to be called Mara, bitter (Ruth 1:20). Ruth bound herself anyway, with an oath in the name of Naomi's God. The church has long borrowed her words for weddings, and the borrowing is fair as long as we remember who said them and why. They're the vow of someone choosing loyalty with her eyes open and nothing to gain, and that's the loyalty a long marriage asks for.

The second passage comes from a poet grieving Jerusalem after Babylon destroyed it. With the city still in ruins, he calls to mind the LORD's loving devotion and finds his mercies new every morning. Your promise today doesn't rest on your record; you'll break it in small ways by Tuesday. It rests on the faithfulness of God, who was witness between you the first time, as the prophet Malachi reminded husbands who had broken faith (Malachi 2:14).

scripture.text: But Ruth replied: “Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you. For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God. Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.”
Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!

questions: What did you promise at your wedding? Copy the words if you found them, or write what you remember.
Which of those promises have you kept well, and which poorly? Be as honest about yourself as you were yesterday.
Knowing what you know now, what would you promise your spouse that you didn't know to promise then?
What is one thing you will stop doing, and one thing you will start, for the sake of your marriage?
What does your marriage need every day, every week, and once a year? Write one practice for each, small enough to keep.
Write your promise to your spouse in your own words, five sentences at most. Speak to them, not about them.
sessions.together:
Read each other your first four answers, then give most of your time to the last two. If your vows used a word like *obey*, talk about what each of you meant by it then and means now, and take any disagreement to your pastor and your church. No vow gives either of you the right to frighten, pressure, or control the other; if a vow has been used that way, stop here and turn to the care note.

Put your lists side by side and agree on three practices, one daily, one weekly, and one yearly, small enough that you'll still keep them in February, such as ten screen-free minutes or a prayer for each other each night, an evening a week that's only yours, and a weekend like this once a year. Write them on a card you'll both see at home.

Then renew your promises. If one of you isn't ready to promise anything today, an honest *not yet* is better than words you don't mean. Otherwise, face each other, take each other's hands, and say what you wrote or the words you said at your wedding, whichever you can say most truthfully. At a church retreat, leaders may gather couples for this; your words are yours to say aloud or keep between you. If you both pray, ask God to help you keep what you can't keep alone. If one of you doesn't, the other may pray aloud while you listen, if that's welcome.
sessions.practice: Today, put your card where you'll both see it, and put the date of your next time away on the calendar before other things claim it. Tell one person you trust what you promised, so someone besides the two of you knows. Then keep the daily practice on Monday night, even if it feels small, and again the night after. Small is how marriages are kept.
